landmark.calloutText:
Know more about the
"Prinsesa ng Baybay"
landmark.title: Ang Prinsesa ng Baybay
landmark.subtitle: The story behind the statue on the Puerto Princesa Baywalk.
landmark.historyHeading: How the statue came to be
history: Ang Prinsesa ng Baybay ("The Princess of the Shore") is the fiberglass statue of a woman with windswept hair, playing with birds, that stands at the far end of the Puerto Princesa Baywalk — the City Coastal Reclamation Area, the city’s own version of Manila’s Roxas Boulevard.

The statue draws on local folklore about how the city got its name: seafarers were said to see a princess-like maiden walking along the bay late in the afternoon or early evening, who would seem to vanish whenever anyone approached. The Rotary Club of Puerto Princesa commissioned the statue in 2007 as a symbol of that story and of Palaweño life and culture more broadly, unveiling it on December 7, 2007.
trivia: The Rotary Club of Puerto Princesa initiated the project in 2007, under then-president Bobby Castro, hoping to give the city a landmark on the scale of Singapore’s Merlion or Denmark’s Little Mermaid.
The design was chosen through a public contest launched on July 13, 2007, under the theme "Simbolo ng Ating Kultura at Buhay" (Symbol of Our Culture and Life).
The winning concept combined designs from two artists: Zaldy Jumawan, then based in Palawan, and Elordie Mesac, a Tagbanua artist trained under Charles Wandag’s Aborlan Arts Program.
The statue’s face was deliberately sculpted with the flat nose characteristic of the Tagbanua people, Puerto Princesa’s original inhabitants.
The final 100-kilogram fiberglass statue was executed by Manila-based sculptor Ronel F. Roces and unveiled on December 7, 2007, at the City Coastal Reclamation Area — the Baywalk.
Both original designers reportedly felt the finished sculpture strayed from their concept of a princess watching the sunset with birds in the background.

miningWatch.title: Mining Watch
miningWatch.subtitle: Tracking how mining is affecting Palawan's environment, communities, and Indigenous peoples.
miningWatch.disclaimer: This page is compiled from independent journalism and human-rights/environmental organizations for public awareness. It is not an official statement or position of the City Government of Puerto Princesa.
miningWatch.mapCaveat: Pins mark known mining sites at the barangay/municipality level, sourced from official MGB records and cited news reporting below — they are approximate locations, not surveyed concession boundaries. Tap a pin for details and sources.
miningWatch.forestLossHeading: Tree Cover Loss by Dominant Driver
miningWatch.forestLossSubtitle: What's actually clearing forest across Palawan province, 2001–2025, by dominant cause — from permanent conversion (agriculture, mining, settlements) to temporary disturbances (logging, fire) that can eventually regrow.
miningWatch.forestLossMiningNote: "Hard commodities" — mining and energy infrastructure — clears the least total area of any driver province-wide: about 1,257 hectares of roughly 224,000 lost since 2001, behind even permanent agriculture and shifting cultivation, which dominate by a wide margin. That number likely understates mining's real footprint: the 11 companies now operating in Palawan hold roughly 29,430 hectares in concessions, most not yet actively cleared, and mining roads open remote forest to logging and farming by others — clearing this chart attributes to those drivers instead, not to mining. Hectares aside, mining also targets old-growth primary forest and protected ancestral domains specifically (Mt. Mantalingahan, Bataraza, Brooke's Point — see the map above), and its damage reaches beyond the cleared footprint through water pollution, like the hexavalent chromium contamination documented near Rio Tuba below.
miningWatch.footerNote: Every article below links to its original, independently published source. If you spot an outdated or broken link, please open an issue on this project's GitHub repository.
context: Palawan is often called the Philippines’ “last ecological frontier” — a UNESCO Man and Biosphere Reserve holding nearly half the country’s remaining old-growth forest, 30 percent of its mangroves, and 40 percent of its coral reefs. It also sits on some of the world’s largest untapped nickel deposits, a mineral in rising global demand for electric-vehicle batteries. That has made large-scale mining one of the most contested issues in the province for decades.

Puerto Princesa itself carries a cautionary chapter: the city was once home to the Palawan Quicksilver Mines Inc. mercury mine, shuttered since 1976, near which residents were later found to test positive for mercury poisoning. In March 2025, the provincial government responded to decades of advocacy by signing a 50-year moratorium on new mining agreements and exploration permits — but the ban doesn’t apply to Puerto Princesa (a highly urbanized city outside provincial jurisdiction), doesn’t affect the 11 mining operations already permitted elsewhere in the province, and leaves the Palawan Council for Sustainable Development able to grant clearances that critics warn could still open the door to new projects.

The articles below — independent journalism and reporting from human-rights and environmental organizations — track how that fight is playing out: in the courts, in Indigenous ancestral domains, and in the rivers and coral reefs downstream of mining operations.
